Oh no: "Sequences must not be used as the type of an attribute or constant. ...  Instead of a writable attribute of a sequence type, it is suggested that a pair of operations to get and set the sequence is used."

https://heycam.github.io/webidl/#idl-sequence

Ah, right, glad Web IDL caught that! We actually want to use `FrozenArray<>`, not `sequence<>`.

This will be a little annoying as we can no longer return a new list every time in the getter (i.e. "Return _elements_.") But that's actually a good fix to make. The spec right now implies that `el.attrElements !== el.attrElements`, because each call of the getter would return a fresh sequence. That's pretty bad behavior.

The most straightforward thing I can think of is to just have a separate slot, call it [[attrElementsCache]] or similar, which stores the last result of the computation logic ("On getting" steps 3-5). Then, still keep those steps to re-compute the _elements_ list, but do a comparison between the _elements_ list and the value of [[attrElementsCache]] before returning. If they're the same, return the cached value (throwing away _elements_). If they're different, reset the cached value to the new _elements_, and return it.

When you use the `FrozenArray<>` syntax, IDL automatically converts any incoming JS iterable into an IDL frozen array. Just like when you use the `sequence<>` syntax, IDL automatically converts any incoming JS iterable into an IDL sequence.

OK, I pushed some editorial work, plus one slight normative change (noted in the commit message) for the frozenarray case. I also properly handled the caching for the frozenarray case, which is annoying (and ideally the IDL spec should make that easier for us, but it doesn't).

One remaining normative question I have is why we have the test

> If element is not a descendant of any of this element's shadow-including ancestors, then continue.

for the frozenarray reflection, but not the single-element reflection. It also seems perhaps redundant with the same-tree (now same-root) checks.

Thanks for the edits! Took me a while to get my head around the change to the `FrozenArray` behaviour, but I got there.

> One remaining normative question I have is why we have the test
> 
> > If element is not a descendant of any of this element's shadow-including ancestors, then continue.
> 
> for the frozenarray reflection, but not the single-element reflection. It also seems perhaps redundant with the same-tree (now same-root) checks.

Here's what I see for single-element reflection:

> On setting, the IDL attribute must perform the following steps:
> - If the given value is not a descendant of any of this element's shadow-including ancestors, then:
>    1. Set this element's explicitly set attr-element to null.
>    2. Remove the content attribute from this element.
>    3. Return.

vs for `FrozenArray`:

> On setting, the IDL attribute must perform the following steps: (...)
> - For each element in the given value:
>    1. If element is not a descendant of any of this element's shadow-including ancestors, then continue.

These are supposed to be analogous, and to avoid being able to set any element reference which is not "visible" to the attribute's element due to Shadow DOM boundaries. The idea is that you can "see out" of Shadow DOM, but not "see into" it.

The same-tree/same-root checks are for reflecting the ID as a string. You can set an element reference which is not in the same tree (but in a tree with a shared ancestor), but it won't reflect to the content attribute.

@annevk One issue we're struggling with is that we don't have any straightforward way of enforcing shadow root boundaries when someone moves an element into a deeper shadow root. e.g. ```html #shadow-root (open) | | #shadow-root (open) | |
| ``` Say we do: ```js input.ariaLabelledByElements = [label]; ``` That's allowed. And we're *not* allowed to do this (regardless of shadow root mode): ```js input.ariaActiveDescendant = div; ``` However, we can legally do this: ```js input.shadowRoot.appendChild(label); ``` That would be a weird thing to do, for sure, but there is nothing stopping us as far as I can tell. My first thought at how to handle this would be to continue to allow `label` to be in `input`'s `aria-labelledby`-associated elements, but not to allow it to be returned by the IDL attribute getter, i.e. ```js console.log(input.ariaLabelledByElements); // logs [] ``` This means that we're going to have to do the scope check for both setting *and* getting the IDL attributes. Does this seem reasonable to you? Do you have any other suggestions, or have I missed something?

Is it expected / part of this feature that elements continue to be associated even when it's removed from the current tree?? That seems rather unexpected. When an element with a given ID gets removed from a tree, ID ref usually stops working.

> Is it expected / part of this feature that elements continue to be associated even when it's removed from the current tree?? That seems rather unexpected. When an element with a given ID gets removed from a tree, ID ref usually stops working.

It's expected that you can refer to elements in "lighter" shadow trees, yes (i.e. where IDREFs would fail to be associated).

It's a consequence of the way Shadow DOM works that there's no effective way to prevent the behaviour I described when moving nodes, since there is no existing machinery to make things behave differently when moving things between shadow trees than moving within the same tree.

> > Is it expected / part of this feature that elements continue to be associated even when it's removed from the current tree?? That seems rather unexpected. When an element with a given ID gets removed from a tree, ID ref usually stops working.
>
> It's expected that you can refer to elements in "lighter" shadow trees, yes (i.e. where IDREFs would fail to be associated).

That's not what I'm talking about. I'm talking about *removing*. When an element is removed from the document (e.g. via `removeChild`), is the element expected to continue to be associated with whatever element it got associated with id-ref arrays?

> That's not what I'm talking about. I'm talking about _removing_. When an element is removed from the document (e.g. via `removeChild`), is the element expected to continue to be associated with whatever element it got associated with id-ref arrays?

Hmm, I must have misunderstood then - I take it this is not in response to my previous comment (https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/3917#issuecomment-527263562) - or at least tangential.

That is a good question. I think as specced right now, it probably would continue to be associated. 

I can see two options:
1. We could specify that `attr`-associated elements are only to be treated as valid (e.g. for `aria-labelledby`, don't include detached elements when computing the name for an element) when they are in the same document. 
2. Or, we could specify that when a node is removed from the document, some clean-up has to occur to remove it from any `attr`-associated element references as well. This would mean keeping track of the relationship in both directions.

On balance, I think I would prefer the first option.

[edit] Though I could see how authors may not expect that stale references to that element would stick around, even if they're not being used, so I could definitely see a strong argument for the second option.

> > That's not what I'm talking about. I'm talking about _removing_. When an element is removed from the document (e.g. via `removeChild`), is the element expected to continue to be associated with whatever element it got associated with id-ref arrays?
> 
> Hmm, I must have misunderstood then - I take it this is not in response to my previous comment ([#3917 (comment)](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/3917#issuecomment-527263562)) - or at least tangential.

It's in response to your comment. Let me explain why.

> I can see two options:
> 
> 1. We could specify that `attr`-associated elements are only to be treated as valid (e.g. for `aria-labelledby`, don't include detached elements when computing the name for an element) when they are in the same document.
> 2. Or, we could specify that when a node is removed from the document, some clean-up has to occur to remove it from any `attr`-associated element references as well. This would mean keeping track of the relationship in both directions.

If we did (2), then it's moving an element from one place to another would have disassociated it (because in order to insert an element somewhere would require first removing it).

I could see the argument either way. (2) would incur an extra runtime cost during DOM tree mutation like live node lists, or some other kind of house keeping like bidirectional mapping as you suggested.

> If we did (2), then it's moving an element from one place to another would have disassociated it (because in order to insert an element somewhere would require first removing it).

Hm, is there no difference between moving an element and removing it from the document? Would moving within the same scope also cause a disassociation?

> > If we did (2), then it's moving an element from one place to another would have disassociated it (because in order to insert an element somewhere would require first removing it).
> 
> Hm, is there no difference between moving an element and removing it from the document? Would moving within the same scope also cause a disassociation?

There is no distinction between moving an element vs. removing & inserting it elsewhere because "moving" an element is defined as removing it from its old parent and inserting under a new parent.

> There is no distinction between moving an element vs. removing & inserting it elsewhere because "moving" an element is defined as removing it from its old parent and inserting under a new parent.

Would you expect moving an element within the same scope to cause it to drop off element reference properties?

e.g.

```html
<input id="input">
<optgroup>
  <option id="first">First option</option>
  <option id="second">Second option</option>
</optgroup>
```

```js
input.ariaActiveDescendantElement = first;
first.parentElement.appendChild(first);  // move to end of list
console.log(input.ariaActiveDescendantElement);  // now null?
```

> > There is no distinction between moving an element vs. removing & inserting it elsewhere because "moving" an element is defined as removing it from its old parent and inserting under a new parent.
> 
> Would you expect moving an element within the same scope to cause it to drop off element reference properties?
> 
> e.g.
> 
> ```
> <input id="input">
> <optgroup>
>   <option id="first">First option</option>
>   <option id="second">Second option</option>
> </optgroup>
> ```
> 
> ```js
> input.ariaActiveDescendantElement = first;
> first.parentElement.appendChild(first);  // move to end of list
> console.log(input.ariaActiveDescendantElement);  // now null?
> ```

That would be the behavior of other normal DOM API.

e.g.
```js
document.body.innerHTML = '<input type="checkbox" form="foo"><form id="foo">';
document.querySelector('input').form; // This would be not null.
document.querySelector('form').remove();
document.querySelector('input').form; // This would be null.
```

If we don't disassociate an element upon removal, we'd get into very strange situations like an input element associated with a form element in a different document, or a single label element associated with multiple input elements in different documents or shadow trees.

That seems to be answering a different question from the one I'm asking.

When you explicitly use an IDREF, and then remove the element with that ID, you can't look up the ID any more. If you did something like...

```js
document.body.innerHTML = '<form id="foo"></form><input type="checkbox" form="foo">';
document.querySelector('input').form; // This would be not null.
document.body.appendChild(document.querySelector('form'));
document.querySelector('input').form; // Same result as before.
```

... technically removing and adding the form, the association is *not* lost.

That code would remove the association and then inserts it back into the DOM, and newly associates it with the form again. That’s one benefit of ID ref referring to whatever element which happens to have the matching string. An explicit association with JS API can’t work like that.

e.g.
```js
document.body.innerHTML = '<form id="foo" title="1"></form><form id="foo" title="2"></form><input type="checkbox" form="foo">';
document.querySelector('input').form.title; // 1.
document.body.appendChild(document.querySelector('form'));
document.querySelector('input').form.title; // 2.
```

I'm still interested in what you would _expect_ in this case:

```html
<input id="input">
<optgroup>
  <option id="first">First option</option>
  <option id="second">Second option</option>
</optgroup>
```

```js
input.ariaActiveDescendantElement = first;
first.parentElement.appendChild(first);  // move to end of list
console.log(input.ariaActiveDescendantElement);  // ?
```

If we went with option 1 in https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/3917#issuecomment-528642778, it would still be `first`. This would be analogous to using a globally-unique ID. I think this behaviour would be less surprising, although it would come at the cost of potential memory leaks under limited circumstances (i.e. authors setting a relationship, then removing the associated element from the DOM without also explicitly resetting the relationship).

If we went with option 2, it would be `null`. This would probably be an unpleasant surprise, but would avoid surprise memory leaks.

> I'm still interested in what you would _expect_ in this case:
> 
> ```
> <input id="input">
> <optgroup>
>   <option id="first">First option</option>
>   <option id="second">Second option</option>
> </optgroup>
> ```
> 
> ```js
> input.ariaActiveDescendantElement = first;
> first.parentElement.appendChild(first);  // move to end of list
> console.log(input.ariaActiveDescendantElement);  // ?
> ```
> 
> If we went with option 1 in [#3917 (comment)](https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/3917#issuecomment-528642778), it would still be `first`.

I'd expect `input.ariaActiveDescendantElement` to be null in that case.

> This would be analogous to using a globally-unique ID.

It's not. ID string simply matches whatever element which happens to be the first element with the same ID string. The way I think of ID ref is that it's referring to an abstract notion of any element with a given ID which appears first in the tree order. I'm not associating it with any particular instance of an element.

With JS API, I'm associating a particular instance of an element, not any abstract notion or relation which ends up resolving to an element as with the case with string based ID referencing.

> I'd expect `input.ariaActiveDescendantElement` to be null in that case.

Could you expand on why this shouldn't be surprising? This would be inconsistent with an element reference in script, which persists regardless of whether an element is moved in the DOM (or even removed).

> With JS API, I'm associating a particular instance of an element, not any abstract notion or relation which ends up resolving to an element as with the case with string based ID referencing.

I agree that that is a difference in practice; I would argue that ID based referencing is _intended_ to be used this way, though (i.e. associating a specific element) - it's an [authoring error](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/dom.html#global-attributes:tree) ("the id attribute value must be unique amongst all the IDs in the element's tree") have multiple elements with the same ID.

(Yes, I am aware that you could remove an ID from one element and put it on another, but again, I think this is against the spirit of the original API.)

> > I'd expect `input.ariaActiveDescendantElement` to be null in that case.
> 
> Could you expand on why this shouldn't be surprising? This would be inconsistent with an element reference in script, which persists regardless of whether an element is moved in the DOM (or even removed).

Because the element got removed? I don't think arguing one or another based on one's opinions is productive here. We need an objective evidence to suggest either behavior is better / more desirable.

> > With JS API, I'm associating a particular instance of an element, not any abstract notion or relation which ends up resolving to an element as with the case with string based ID referencing.
> 
> I agree that that is a difference in practice; I would argue that ID based referencing is _intended_ to be used this way

I disagree.

Ugh... after today’s discussion, I noticed a new issue with this current proposal. We can’t really do “invalidation” either during insertion, removal, or on get if it’s a frozen array since we can’t mutate an array without potentially executing arbitrary scripts.

So these properties probably need to be a new subclass of NodeList which auto-updates, or these IDL attributes need to be replaced by getter/setter pairs where getting would return a new array each time.
Can you explain why changing the value returned by the property could run arbitrary scripts?

> Hm... do we want to remove duplicates from FrozenArray upon assignment (setter) here?

I'm not sure I follow. IDREF-list attributes don't disallow duplicate values as far as I know; unless there's a specific reason to disallow them here, I don't understand why we would add that constraint. (I also can't see any reason why authors would want to be able to use duplicate values, but I'm not that imaginative.)

`DOMTokenList` de-duplicates the entires. e.g.
```
span = document.createElement('span');
span.className = 'foo bar foo'
span.classList.length // 2
span.classList[0] // foo
span.classList[1] // bar
span.classList.value // foo bar foo
```

> span.className = 'foo bar foo'
> span.classList.length // 2
> span.classList[0] // foo
> span.classList[1] // bar
> span.classList.value // foo bar foo

Thanks for that!

I think in that case de-duplicating makes sense, because the classlist is really more of a class set - adding another _instance of the same_ class, or changing the order, wouldn't make a difference.

With an IDREF list, the order is significant, and adding a duplicate entry would change the behaviour.

For example, if I had something like `aria-labelelledby="foo foo"`, that should cause the contents of the `"foo"` element to be included twice in the name of the element with the `aria-labelledby` attribute on it.

Hm... that's interesting. In the case of [slot assignment](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/3534), we need to remove duplicates but that doesn't really have a setter so it works fine there, and I guess there aren't really any other DOM API that uses ID ref list than ARIA?

There is: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#attr-tdth-headers. That's currently defined to take an unordered set and there's no API for it that would expose order or some such. I guess this would be the first ordered list of IDs. (Note that `DOMTokenList` is ordered, but it's indeed a set despite the name, not a list.)

This PR has been on hold for more than a year now, so let's do an update.

Chromium and WebKit have now an implementation of this PR under a runtime flag (`AOMAriaRelationshipProperties` flag in Chromium and `AriaReflectionForElementReferencesEnabled` flag in WebKit).
Both implementations allow to refer to descendants of your shadow-including ancestors (https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/6063).

There's a WPT test covering this PR too: https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/blob/master/dom/nodes/aria-element-reflection.tentative.html (Chromium [fails one case](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=1321564) but that's being currently fixed).

Does anyone remember what's blocking this PR? What else should be done before being ready to merge? Thanks!
